analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators set safety standards for guns and ammunition, like they already can for other products.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lists guns and ammunition as the one consumer product the Consumer Product Safety Commission is barred from regulating. This bill would delete that exclusion, letting the Commission write safety standards for firearms and ammunition the way it does for toys, cribs, and power tools. It was referred to a subcommittee the day after it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would benefit people exposed to defective or unreasonably dangerous firearm and ammunition designs, since the CPSC could for the first time require design changes, warnings, or recalls. Consumers generally would gain a safety net that exists for every other household product.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to unsafe firearm designs

how_it_helps.text: By deleting the firearms exclusion from the Consumer Product Safety Act, the bill would allow the Consumer Product Safety Commission to issue federal safety standards for pistols, revolvers, other firearms, shells, and cartridges [S2, S3].

Guns are currently the only major consumer product the CPSC cannot set safety rules for; the bill would close that gap, potentially reducing accidental deaths and injuries from defective firearm designs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on firearms and ammunition manufacturers, who would have to meet federal safety standards, modify designs, and face recalls — costs that could be passed to gun buyers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Firearms are unlike most consumer products, and critics have long argued that CPSC safety jurisdiction could become a vehicle for design restrictions that go beyond ordinary safety rules; this is why the exclusion has been in law since the statute's creation [S3].
The bill was never considered by the full committee or debated on the floor, so its actual design and costs were never weighed publicly in Congress [S1, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a narrow, single-purpose change with a modest goal: letting a safety agency do for guns what it already does for other products. The main cost is to the firearms industry, which would face federal design standards, and to gun-rights advocates who argue safety regulation could shade into functional restrictions. Its death means guns remain the only consumer product whose safety design is largely exempt from federal review.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee on the day after introduction and never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Robin Kelly (D-IL) introduced the bill on June 20, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1, S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate, and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, who remain exempt from federal consumer product safety standards. Nobody else gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms manufacturers keeping their regulatory exemption

for.name: Rep. Robin Kelly (D-IL)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove the firearms exclusion from consumer product safety law.

for.name: 12 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Consumer Product Safety Commission jurisdiction over firearms and championed the original statutory exclusion; its opposition has long made such bills politically hazardous for committee chairs.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced out of a Republican-controlled House committee [S1, S4].

industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's unique exemption from consumer product safety regulation, exposing firearm designs to federal safety standards and potential recalls [S2, S3]. Its failure preserved that exemption.
